speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the sponsors of the Bill of Rights, Hon. Noel Dorion, expressed recently a few reservations with regard to the effectiveness of that bill in practice. The purpose of this bill is to remedy a situation. Too many police officers violate the Bill of Rights every day; too many police officers treat prisoners like dirt.
Consequently, the object of this bill is to make it a criminal offence for a police officer or any law officer to refuse a prisoner the right to call his lawyer.

Newfoundland Terms of Union a portion of the understanding by which Newfoundland became the tenth province of Canada. Coming as I do from one of the Atlantic provinces and in view of the fact that the province of Newfoundland is one of the others, I have no hesitation in saying that I have a special personal interest in any statute designed to benefit any province in that group.
Having a special interest, I can say to the house that I remember well the feeling of satisfaction which we in New Brunswick had when the Terms of Union with Newfoundland were arrived at in the year 1949, even though we constituted the opposition party in the New Brunswick legislature. It was our feeling at that time-and subsequent events have proved we were right-that the entry of Newfoundland into Canada was going to be of special benefit to the provinces on the Atlantic seaboard, which up to that time had been known as the maritime provinces and which, with the entry of Newfoundland into the confederation, became known more properly as the Atlantic provinces.
After 1952, when we were favoured with a greater degree of responsibility in New Brunswick than previously, we frequently became associated on an official, personal and, I believe, friendly basis with Premier Smallwood of Newfoundland and members of his cabinet. Our relationship was on a most cordial basis and we found ourselves willing and anxious to work together with Premier Smallwood as well as with the other premiers of the Atlantic provinces.
I learned from Premier Smallwood at first hand the importance he attached to term 29 and it is of more than passing interest that the commission which was appointed as a result of term 29 was headed by the chief justice of New Brunswick, Hon. J. B. McNair. I am sure it is of some interest to the house to know how such an amount was divided among the four Atlantic provinces. We were told at that time that our financial advisers in each province should get together and agree on an acceptable distribution. They met in Halifax and spent several days discussing the matter. I naturally received frequent reports of their deliberations and the points raised by representatives of all the provinces. Out of those discussions came a recommendation to their respective governments that the $25 million per year special adjustment grants be made to the Atlantic provinces on the basis of $7,500,000 each to Newfoundland, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, and $2,500,000 to the province of Prince Edward Island.
This is the basis on which the amounts were finally awarded and this arrangement continued for a period of four years. subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR ALLOWANCES TO PERSONS BEING TRAINED
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is a great honour for me to bring before the house this resolution preceding a bill to increase training allowances for unemployed workers and certain other classes of workers.
I believe, Mr. Chairman, that our modern industrial society is very pleased with the improvements in industrial production techniques, which result in a greatly increased productivity and in the enrichment of society as a whole.
However, we must keep in mind that in this process of improving production techniques, some people are affected; this means that workers who have been trained for an industry or techniques which are now obsolete, find themselves, sometimes at an early age, without jobs and facing an indefinite unemployment.
May 18, 1966



The resolution introduces a measure which concerns the crucial problem of the retraining and further training of our labour force. As the Economic Council of Canada has pointed out, there is a need for a major effort to improve the skills of existing members of the labour force, and one of the reasons why existing training programs have not been used to a greater extent is the inadequacy of present training allowances. The measure with which this resolution is concerned is intended, among other things, to assist provincial governments to remedy this defect.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
I think it is impossible to overemphasize the importance of training in today's rapidly changing world. Many of us know from our own experience and that of an increasing number of others that our skills and knowledge can quickly become out of date. New situations and new needs almost constantly test our ability to adapt and adjust in the dynamic working world of today.
Many people have enough basic education and broad skills to be able to meet these challenges, but a distressing proportion of adults in this country do not, and so become unemployed or are threatened with the loss of their job. There is another important aspect to this urgent problem. The Economic Council of Canada has documented very fully the training gap which exists in Canada as compared to the United States, and has shown its influence on income levels in the two countries. This training gap must be narrowed if we are to achieve our own goals of economic and social development and if the qualifications of those now in the labour force are to catch up with the needs of tomorrow's employment.
We will not solve these problems unless the community as a whole takes a new attitude toward the importance of training. We all have to recognize that rapid change and growth must lead us to regard training as a normal and productive part of people's working lives. When we all recognize this, we will have gone a long way toward overcoming the inhibitions of those who have the least selfconfidence and the greatest need for training. We must therefore raise the status of training. There are many factors that influence status, but certainly pay is one of the most important. That basic fact is recognized in the measure proposed in this resolution. In
23033-334 i
Vocational and Technical Training effect it equates training with work rather than with unemployment and welfare.
The essential purpose of the proposal is to break the connection between training and unemployment. Up to now, unemployed workers who went into training courses have continued to receive unemployment insurance benefits during training. These benefits are deducted from the training allowances otherwise provided, so that the allowances are in effect merely a supplement.
Thus people up to now have had to use up their unemployment insurance protection while in training. On occasion, if they cannot obtain a job immediately after completing their course, they find themselves with no benefit at all or with their protection greatly reduced. They may find themselves worse off than if they had not taken training but had stayed inactive for a time and then got a job. I believe this is wrong. It treats training as equivalent to unemployment rather than to work. It penalizes a person for taking training, whereas we should offer him an incentive. It lowers, instead of raising, the whole status of training.
The measure proposed in this resolution breaks the dependence of training on unemployment insurance. It provides that any unemployed worker who enters a training course covered by a federal-provincial agreement will be entitled to a training allowance and will retain intact his unemployment insurance benefit and contribution rights. When he leaves such a training course, he will have exactly the same amount of unemployment insurance protection as when he entered, even if the training course is as long as two years in duration.
Hitherto the incomes of people in training have come partly from unemployment insurance, if they were entitled to such benefits, and partly from training allowances. The benefits are financed from the federal unemployment insurance fund. The allowances are paid by provincial governments but the federal government reimburses 90 per cent of the expenditure.
Obviously this financial system has to be changed when the connection between training and unemployment insurance is severed. The proposed measure will in effect substitute for unemployment insurance a basic training allowance for which the federal government will reimburse the provinces 100 per cent. The amount of this proposed basic allowance will be $35 a week. In effect, since training courses are normally 35 hours a
5278	COMMONS
Vocational and Technical Training week, it is a minimum rate of a dollar an hour for training. It replaces unemployment insurance for trainees. It will be available to people in training courses if they have previously been unemployed or if they are referred to training courses when they have previously been self-employed in primary industries such as farming, fishing or logging. In addition, the federal government will continue to reimburse the provinces for 90 per cent of training allowances in excess of the basic $35 a week.
The amount of these additional allowances is a matter for each province to decide in accordance with its own needs, wage levels and priorities. The rules governing the supplementary allowances will therefore be determined in the agreements negotiated with each province. We propose to fix a maximum supplementary allowance of $55 a week, which with the basic $35 would mean a total allowance of $90 a week.
At the federal-provincial conference at which we discussed this matter last January, there was general agreement among provincial ministers as to the desirability of increasing the level of allowances. We anticipate that the maximum total allowance of $90 a week will be paid to trainees with a number of dependants living in the relatively high-wage areas of the country. Lower scales will be provided where wage levels are lower, and there will probably also be variations according to whether the trainee lives at home or has to be away in order to attend his training course.
In negotiating the agreements with us, each province will be able to decide whether its needs are best met by a uniform scale of allowances for the province or, as may be the case in the larger provinces particularly, by regional variations in the scales. We will be willing to support any reasonable system providing variations according to family circumstances and living costs, provided the total allowance is never less than the basic $35 and that the supplement in which we share does not exceed a maximum of a further $55 a week. This flexibility means that it will be possible for the total allowances everywhere to accord to training the importance it deserves without, however, being distorted in relation to wage levels in different areas.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
As was made public at the time, we discussed the outline of these proposals with provincial ministers last January, and my
[Mr. Marchand.l
DEBATES	May 18, 1966
officials have had further discussions with their officers over recent weeks. All provinces are in sympathy with this measure.
I would like to summarize, then, what this measure is intended to do. It will make possible substantially increased training allowances for unemployed workers and for self-employed people who are under-employed in the primary industries. It will provide a basic training allowance of $35 a week for everybody in this category, the cost of which the federal government will bear completely. It will provide additional allowances as deemed appropriate by the provinces, of which the federal government will pay 90 per cent to an agreed maximum amount. It will preserve the unemployment insurance rights of workers during the training period. It will thus break the identification of training with unemployment. It will recognize the status that training ought to have in our contemporary industrial world.
In short, I feel that this proposal will be a significant help in giving training the importance it ought to have, in response to the needs of modern technology and the requirements of a modern economy. Most important of all, it will give individual workers the encouragement and the practical opportunity of upgrading their basic knowledge, of replacing obsolete skills, and of strengthening existing qualifications. Higher incomes and better working careers will be the result for the individual, while greater economic and social growth will be the result for the nation.
We have many other tasks to accomplish, but this measure will carry us forward to an important degree toward our goal of developing and fully utilizing the great human resources of our country.

That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of an early amendment to the Criminal Code of Canada making it an offence, punishable by fine or imprisonment or both, to in Canada manufacture or distribute or be in possession of motor vehicle master key sets, or import the same into Canada, save by the manufacturer or the assembler of the said motor vehicles or by such person or persons duly authorized by the said manufacturer or assembler.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the subject matter of my motion this afternoon is not exactly world shattering. I suggest, however, that the impact on the population of Canada of what I am trying to get at could be very great. We all know that every year thousands of motor vehicles are stolen from the streets, from garages, some to reappear but many to disappear forever. The loss to private individuals, corporations and the insurance companies with whom the owners of these motor vehicles have theft insurance mounts into the hundreds of thousands of dollars, perhaps millions every year.
What I am trying to do is to prevent at least a portion of this loss as a result of what is now being introduced into Canada, to which the general public has access, so that we can cut down on these occurrences. I am not holding any brief at all for the motorist who is foolish enough to leave his car parked on the street or in an unlocked garage with the keys in the ignition. He is inviting trouble. Nor is what I am going to suggest going to guard against the man who is going to break into a vehicle and either use a steel wire or some other form of contact with the ignition to get the car going. What I am getting at is something that has come to the attention of Chambers of Commerce, the Association of Chiefs of Police of Canada and to the All Canada Insurance Federation as a result of advertising which has appeared in eastern Canada.
Actually, these advertisements were brought to the attention of my correspondent by the Better Business Bureau of Edmonton.

My reason in bringing this resolution forward has to do with the inquiry made by the Association of Police Chiefs in Canada of the postal authorities of Canada as to whether there is any way of stopping the distribution of these key sets. The association feared that the investment of $15 needed to buy these key sets would yield handsome dividends to even a minor car theft ring.
We all know that those who wish to steal a car have to do a number of things to it before they steal it. Time is taken by a person endeavouring to get in a car, in tinkering with it. During that time he may be discovered. But if one is in possession of a master key set, and if he can go up to any Chevrolet, Pontiac or Chrysler or, in fact, any automobile made in North America, and just open the door and drive off, the chances of apprehension are exceedingly small. In addition, when the automobile later has to be disposed of there are no signs that the law has been broken; there are no signs of unlawful entry through the breaking of a small vent window, or of damage to the rubber alongside those windows.
My motion seeks to make the possession, manufacture or distribution of these key sets an offence under the Criminal Code. I have not mentioned what section shall be amended. I simply ask the government to consider the advisability of amending the code. In parenthesis, might I suggest that the sections of the code to be amended might be those dealing with the theft of motor vehicles, or those dealing with such offences as having in possession a motor vehicle without consent of the lawful owner.
What I am getting at is that it should be illegal and punishable both by fine and/or imprisonment to manufacture, distribute, or actually be in possession of a motor vehicle master key set, or to import the same into Canada, save by the manufacturer or the assembler of the said motor vehicle, or by such person or persons duly authorized by the said manufacturer or assembler to have those keys.

In any town or city of Canada police authorities ought to be in possession of a master key set to be used with respect to motor vehicles. For instance if a motorist is unfortunate enough to lose his keys, he might refer to the principal garage, or to the principal agency or police authority in the community and, after properly identifying himself to the representative of the garage, agency, or police authority, have his motor vehicle opened without the necessity of breaking the lock. After that he could either have a new key made, or have a new lock with keys furnished to him.
This sort of thing is permissible under the resolution. The persons helping the motorist would be those who are duly authorized to be in possession of key sets by the manufacturer or assembler. I do not want to make it more inconvenient for motorists to obtain lawfully duplicate keys to the locks of their cars, after they have lost the original keys. Nor do I want motorists to be put to the additional expense of having to break locks.
I am sure, having regard to the representations of the Better Business Bureaux, they would agree with the aims of the resolution. Certainly the All Canada Insurance Federation would agree with the aims of the resolution. I have correspondence from that body addressed to representatives of the insurance branch of the Edmonton Chamber of Commerce, to this effect.
I have sought the opinion of the postal authorities with respect to these keys. Those authorities acknowledged that they had been approached by the Association of Police Chiefs, when the chiefs had their annual convention last year. The postal authorities informed the police chiefs that there was nothing illegal about the manufacture or distribution of key sets by individuals. Therefore the postal authorities could do nothing about controlling the distribution. On the other hand, if it were an offense under the Criminal Code to manufacture, distribute or import such key sets, or such master key sets, except where those actions were authorized by the manufacturer, assembler, or other persons authorized by such manufacturer or assembler, the postal authorities could stop the distribution.
It was pointed out that the key sets were advertised as being available on a C.O.D. basis. Therefore those sending the key sets were utilizing the mails for the transmission and distribution of such master key sets. I do not wish to belabour the point, Mr. Speaker.
May 18, 1966

While the subject matter I have spoken about for the last 15 minutes is not the most important subject matter in the ambit of government business, yet it is one of those matters with which we should concern ourselves. Suppression of these key sets will assist us in the maintenance of law and order. This resolution will not eliminate car thefts, but it will make it more difficult or, at least, it will not make it any easier, to steal cars if we can ban the indiscriminate sales of such master key sets.
I have no idea how many key sets have been sold. I have not had any indication from the police whether people they have apprehended in car thefts have been found in possession of such master key sets. That is immaterial. What we must do is stop dissemination of these sets from the very beginning. There is a legal use for such master key sets. Certainly, there is a much wider illegal use. It is against that illegal use that this resolution is aimed. I ask all hon. members in this house to support the resolution.

speechtext:
The
resolution reads:
That, in the opinion oi this House, the government should consider the advisability of an early amendment to the Criminal Code of Canada making it an offense, punishable by fine or imprisonment or both, to in Canada manufacture or distribute or be in possession of motor vehicle master key sets, or import the same into Canada, save by the manufacturer or the assembler of the said motor vehicles or by such person or persons duly authorized by the said manufacturer or assembler.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
On reading this resolution one could immediately come to the conclusion that the question is one capable of a simple remedy by merely amending the Criminal Code-that merely by amending the code the problem would be solved. Like all proposals of a remedial nature this sounds plausible until you come up against the difficulty of enforcing the law without undue hardship to a lot of other people.
I appreciate the intention of the hon. member who moved this motion; I am sure he is to be commended. But I wonder whether the resolution in its present form is really the answer. Nevertheless I congratulate the hon. member for bringing this matter to the attention of parliament. It may have a salutary effect in the country when people hear about it. However, it seems to me that, as is the case when we consider the enforcement of automobile safety, this is a problem capable of no easy solution.
Criminal Code
I should like to point out that when 7 million cars are on the highways of Canada there are bound to be duplicate keys available to fit cars shipped to different parts of the country. Manufacturers do provide duplicate keys for automobiles. Moreover, there is no difficulty whatever in having such keys made by any locksmith or at any garage. To my knowledge automobile manufacturers do not produce motor vehicle master key sets. What they do manufacture are the keys that go with the car, and duplicates of the same. As a matter of fact, manufacturers make cars with locks which are exactly the same on a great number of vehicles shipped to different parts of Canada.
How likely is it that the prohibition of master keys by law would reduce the number of car thefts? The great majority of drivers today are careful. They are properly trained and capable of looking after their own vehicles. But some accidents do happen. Again, when one considers the number of vehicles on the road-7 millions on the highways of Canada-he can only expect that a great number of duplicate keys would be available to provide service for car owners.
It is true, as the hon. member pointed out, that many cars are stolen every year. But I would remind him that it is not necessary to have a key in order to steal a car. As a matter of record, the largest number of thefts of vehicles is accomplished without the aid of keys. You do not need a key in order to steal a car. All you need do is to pull out some of the ignition wires and join them together.
Duplicate keys are made available for the benefit of the automobile owner who happens to lose one. I dare say that there are many members of this house who at one time or another have lost a car key and found it necessary to go to a garage or to a locksmith to have a new one made. All that is required is a knowledge of the number stamped on each key. I honestly believe that before we embark on the introduction of an amendment to the Criminal Code to make it an offence to be in possession of a duplicate key or a master key, call it what you will, we should consider the difficulties which would be imposed on automobile owners should they happen to lose their own keys. I suggest that before we do anything rash we should give this question further consideration.
It is all very well to seek to bring in amendments to the Criminal Code covering various offences. But we should also be mindful of the way in which such amendments

May 18. 1866
Criminal Code
might conflict with the best interests of the majority of the people affected. As I say, I commend the mover of this motion, but as one who knows something about the automobile business-and I have been in this business for a great number of years-I cannot support the motion in its present form.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
I am all for the protection of car owners, of course. I should like to see every thief who tries to steal a car put behind bars. I have seen a number of them and I have no brief for them at all. At the same time, let us be practical. I repeat, I admire the hon. member's regard for the welfare of automobile owners. Every time I hear someone speak on behalf of automobile owners my heart goes out to him, because for many years I made my living selling automobiles, and I still have a little interest in that business. Therefore I can say that, though I appreciate the intent of the motion, and commend the mover of it, nevertheless I would not be fair to myself, knowing something about the business, if I were to say that I support the motion in its present form.
1 hope the hon. member will have an opportunity to give this matter more serious consideration. If he does, in all probability he will come up with something which would be more in line with the reality of the situation with regard to the theft of automobiles. The best thing we can do at present is discuss the motion, and perhaps at a future date, following greater study of the case, we will be able to support it.

Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure for me to rise this afternoon in support of the motion of the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), although I must admit that when first looking at the formidable preamble to the motion, it did not appear very interesting. Since I had some work to do in my office I was on my way out of the chamber, but I did catch some of the hon. member's remarks and they raised some very intriguing questions.
He has an excellent point when he indicates that some protection should be afforded the car owning public from this sort of advertising and the easy availability of keys of this type. I think the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Badanai), when he pointed out the difficulties that would be encountered by car owners, may have been overstating the case because we do have legislation at present whereby if you are caught in somebody's

house at one o'clock in the morning, with a jimmy in your hand, and you say you are there to look for termites, you wind up in the hoosegow. Therefore I think a great deal depends on where one is found with these instruments, and at what time he is caught.
Our laws are fairly reasonable, in the sense that it would be simple enough to determine whether these keys are in proper or improper hands. Naturally the hon. member for Fort William has a concern, because of his connection with the automobile business. I too have some concern, having latterly been in the laundromat business. The spectre of laundromat keys being easily obtained by every citizen in this country does not arouse any particular enthusiasm in my breast.
I was interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Edmonton West at the conclusion of his statement, and I felt he was rather deprecating the importance of the issue he brought before us today because, just as the atom bomb indicated war was no longer safe with that type of weapon at the disposal of armies, the same thing applies when keys of this type are easily available. There does not seem to be much point in any of us bothering to lock our cars any more. The only solution may be to have a massive return to honesty.
However, I am quite serious in my support of the motion when I hear that such advertisements are permitted to be published in Canada, and that nobody takes a look at the implications of this type of advertising, the kind of thing it can lead to and the kind of encouragement it provides for those who already have sufficient inducement to break the law. For that reason it would be most valuable to pass this motion tonight, amending the Criminal Code to indicate that we do not approve of this type of material being made available to everyone although, as the motion points out, those who have a legitimate purpose for the possession of such keys would still be free to have them. I certainly commend this motion to all hon. members.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to join with other hon. members in commending the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) for presenting this motion to amend the Criminal Code. As he explained, it is designed to prevent entry into locked vehicles and the theft of cars and trucks. On the surface such an amendment to the Criminal Code could be considered as a step toward making the committing of such crimes more difficult.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
The question which arises in my mind, as has been pointed out by the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Badanai), concerns the practical application of such an amendment and the enforcement of this addition to the Criminal Code. Also I think perhaps one point has been lost sight of and that is the original purpose for the designing, manufacturing and supplying of master key sets. Most certainly it never was set up to make it easy for car theft criminals to practise their nefarious occupation. This item was brought forward for a very practical use by those engaged in the manufacture, sale, repair, and servicing of cars and trucks.
In his amendment the hon. member has suggested that in addition to the manufacturer or assembler of motor vehicles being authorized to be in possession of master key sets, the authorization also would include-and it is a bit vague-such person or persons duly authorized by the said manufacturer or assembler. By coincidence I too have had some
Criminal Code
several years experience both at the manufacturing and retail end of the automobile business. I, perhaps, can give you some indication of the practical and quite legitimate use of master key sets by the people who are engaged in this type of business.
Most certainly it would be logical to extend permission and authorization for possession to such people as the authorized dealers throughout the country, of which there are several thousand. It would also be most logical to extend permission and authorization for possession of master key sets to all the service and repair garages throughout the country; it would be most logical to extend this type of authorization to service stations. You could add to that police officers and agencies engaged in the rental or leasing of vehicles, or those engaged in the legitimate sales occupation involved in the merchandising of used vehicles. These occupations all involve legitimate and practical application of master key sets.
Let me give you an example of what happens when one is engaged in a business which carries a stock of a wide diversity of makes, models, and years of cars and trucks. We have a tough climate in various parts of this country, where the weather gets very cold. In the business where such a stock is carried, each vehicle has to be started and operated every day to keep it in goood condition. This means that someone has to carry the keys to each individual vehicle in the process of going through a stock of 60, 70, or in some cases 100 or 150 cars in the course of a morning.
You can imagine the number of keys this person would have to carry with him were he not authorized to have master key sets. Of course this extends to all the other legitimate users such as authorized dealers, service stations, and all those engaged in the repair of automobiles and trucks. I do not think anyone would deny it would be legitimate to authorize these people to have key sets, and by the time you had added up the number of people who legally should be in possession of them, you would have literally thousands and thousands of agents and individuals throughout this country.
As the hon. member for Fort William pointed out, duplicate keys can be cut in several places in practically every town, village and city. They can be duplicated on machines which are quite inexpensive to obtain. I submit that the determined vehicle thief can find ways to steal vehicles without

May 18. 1966
Criminal Code
keys. He does not need door keys or ignition keys if he is determined to steal vehicles. Naturally any legislation which makes it more difficult to obtain master key sets also would inhibit such criminals to some degree; but nevertheless I think-and this is where the problem lies in the amendment-the law would be most difficult to enforce and it certainly would not be long before contraband duplicate master key sets could be obtained by anyone who seriously desired to obtain them.
For this reason, although the intent is most commendable, I really cannot see any benefit in this amendment in respect of preventing vehicle thefts by organized groups of professional criminals. Most certainly such people would have little or no difficulty in obtaining master key sets. Again, at first glance it would seem that it would make it much more difficult for the type of person who probably could be described as a casual, impulsive thief, and the danger of thefts by this type of person might be diminished. But how many vehicle thefts result from the use of master key sets; how many of these master key sets are or ever will be in the possession of the type of person who might be a casual thief? I submit that such determined types as those who now possess such keys still would find it possible, indeed quite easy, to obtain them.
I am all for any practical and enforceable law which will prevent crime. However, I am always a little concerned about the addition to existing laws or laws which are not practical and which perhaps are very difficult to enforce. I sincerely feel that this suggested amendment falls into that category. I believe it probably has a great deal more psychological than practical effect. Unfortunately, I feel I should bring to your attention also the tremendous inconvenience this would cause to those persons who are engaged in the manufacture, sale, repair and servicing of vehicles, who legitimately require these master key sets. In this connection I think I would have to describe it as being about ten pounds of prevention to provide half an ounce of cure.
Again I commend the hon. member for Edmonton West for the intent in his amendment, but in its present form I would find it difficult to support this motion.
